kumis.name: Kumis
kumis.summary: Traditional fermented drink made from mare's milk, central to Turkic and Mongolic peoples of the Central and East Asian steppes, also called airag, with a higher alcohol content than kefir.

tandoor.name: Tandoor
tandoor.summary: Large vase-shaped clay oven, used since antiquity across South Asia, Western Asia, Central Asia and the Horn of Africa to bake flatbreads and roast meat at temperatures up to 480°C.

haloxylon.name: Saxaul
haloxylon.summary: A genus of desert shrubs or small trees, used as fuel in Central Asia.

samsa-food.name: Samsa
samsa-food.summary: A savoury Central Asian pastry, typically a bun stuffed with meat and baked in a clay tandoor oven.

beshbarmak.name: Beshbarmak
beshbarmak.summary: Traditional Central Asian dish of boiled meat, noodles and onion broth, whose name means "five fingers" for the practice of eating it by hand.

dastarkh-n.name: Dastarkhan
dastarkh-n.summary: A traditional dining space used across Central and South Asia, originally a tablecloth spread on the ground or floor as a clean surface for food.

chorba.name: Chorba
chorba.summary: A broad class of stews and rich soups found across North Africa, the Middle East, Turkey, Central Asia and South Asia, sometimes served as a broth or with bread.

pilaf.name: Pilaf
pilaf.summary: A rice or wheat dish cooked in stock with spices and other ingredients, spread widely from the Abbasid Caliphate and known regionally as pilov, polow, pulao or paella.

teahouse.name: Chaikhana
teahouse.summary: An establishment serving tea and light refreshments that often functions as a center of social interaction, much like a coffee house.

bukhara.name: Bukhara
bukhara.summary: Ancient Silk Road city in what is now Uzbekistan, a major center of Islamic scholarship and birthplace of Imam Bukhari, later capital of the Emirate of Bukhara until 1920.

shaybanids.name: Shaybanids
shaybanids.summary: An Uzbek dynasty descended from Genghis Khan's grandson Shiban that ruled the khanates of Bukhara, Khwarezm and Sibir across Central Asia in the 15th and 16th centuries.

po-i-kalyan.name: Po-i-Kalyan
po-i-kalyan.summary: An Islamic religious complex in Bukhara, Uzbekistan, made up of a mosque, minaret and madrasah, with one of Central Asia's largest congregational mosques.

kalyan-minaret.name: Kalyan Minaret
kalyan-minaret.summary: A minaret of the Po-i-Kalyan mosque complex in Bukhara, Uzbekistan, built in 1127; Genghis Khan reportedly spared it when his forces destroyed the rest of the city.

samarkand.name: Samarkand
samarkand.summary: A major city in southeastern Uzbekistan and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Central Asia, a key Silk Road center once capital of the Achaemenid satrapy of Sogdiana.

registan.name: Registan
registan.summary: A historic public square in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, the ceremonial and commercial heart of the Timurid Empire, famed for its three ornately tiled madrasas.

ulugh-beg-madrasa.name: Ulugh Beg Madrasa
ulugh-beg-madrasa.summary: An Islamic school built in Samarkand between 1417 and 1421 by the astronomer-ruler Ulugh Beg, forming part of the Registan and now its oldest surviving building.

qing-dynasty.name: Qing dynasty
qing-dynasty.summary: Manchu-led imperial dynasty of China from 1644 to 1912, the last imperial dynasty, which at its height controlled more territory than any other dynasty in Chinese history.

mongol-bow.name: Mongol bow
mongol-bow.summary: A recurved composite bow historically used in Mongolia and by Mongol Empire horse archers, largely replaced from the 17th century onward by the similar Manchu bow.

gelug.name: Gelug
gelug.summary: The youngest of the four major schools of Tibetan Buddhism, founded by Je Tsongkhapa (1357-1419), which became the dominant school in Tibet and Mongolia by the late 16th century.

sherdar-madrasa.name: Sherdar Madrasa
sherdar-madrasa.summary: A 17th-century Islamic school on the Registan in Samarkand, built 1619–1636, known for its tiger-lion mosaic facade.

tilakari-madrasa.name: Tilakari Madrasa
tilakari-madrasa.summary: A 17th-century Islamic school on the Registan square in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, nicknamed the 'Gilded Madrasa' for its decoration.

khiva.name: Khiva
khiva.summary: A roughly 2,500-year-old city in Uzbekistan, former capital of Khwarezmia and the Khanate of Khiva, whose old town Itchan Kala was Central Asia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.

khanate-of-khiva.name: Khanate of Khiva
khanate-of-khiva.summary: An Uzbek monarchy centered on the city of Khiva in the Khorezm oasis, ruling from 1511 to 1920 (with a mid-1700s interruption) before becoming a Russian protectorate and later Soviet territory.

manchu-bow.name: Manchu bow
manchu-bow.summary: A composite reflex bow used across Manchuria, China, Mongolia and Tibet, known for its long draw and armor-piercing power, which Manchu forces preferred over firearms until the late 19th century.

zanabazar.name: Zanabazar
zanabazar.summary: First Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, Mongolia's supreme Buddhist spiritual leader (1635–1723), named at age four and later recognized by the 5th Dalai Lama; also a noted sculptor and scholar.

zaya-pandita.name: Zaya Pandita
zaya-pandita.summary: A Mongolian Tibetan Buddhist missionary and scholar of Oirat origin, considered the most prominent Oirat Buddhist scholar, credited with inventing the Clear Script.

maqsurah.name: Maqsurah
maqsurah.summary: An enclosed screen near a mosque's mihrab, originally meant to shield a Muslim ruler from assassination during prayer.

iwan.name: Iwan
iwan.summary: A rectangular, usually vaulted hall walled on three sides with one end open, a form of pre-Islamic Iranian origin that became common in Islamic architecture.

itchan-kala.name: Itchan Kala
itchan-kala.summary: The walled inner town of Khiva, Uzbekistan, a World Heritage Site since 1990 with more than 50 historic monuments, mostly from the 18th and 19th centuries.

juma-mosque-khiva.name: Juma Mosque, Khiva
juma-mosque-khiva.summary: A mosque in Khiva, Uzbekistan, first documented in the 10th century and rebuilt in 1788, notable for its hypostyle hall of 212 wooden columns.

dzungar-people.name: Dzungars
dzungar-people.summary: The Oirat Mongol tribes who formed the Dzungar Khanate in the 17th and 18th centuries, also known as Eleuths or Kalmyks, with descendants today in Mongolia, China, Russia and Kazakhstan.

east-turkestan.name: East Turkestan
east-turkestan.summary: A geographical term, coined in the 19th century, for a region in northwestern China now also used by Uyghur separatists for present-day Xinjiang.

qianlong-emperor.name: Qianlong Emperor
qianlong-emperor.summary: Fifth emperor of the Qing dynasty, reigning from 1735 to 1796, who expanded Chinese territory into Inner Asia, including conquering Xinjiang from the Dzungar Khanate.

xinjiang.name: Xinjiang
xinjiang.summary: An autonomous region in northwestern China at the crossroads of Central and East Asia, historically called Chinese Turkestan, crossed by the Silk Road and home to Uyghurs and other ethnic groups.

orenburg.name: Orenburg
orenburg.summary: A Russian city near the Europe-Asia boundary, founded in the 18th century, historically a hub for Kazakh-Russian trade and briefly capital of the Kazakh ASSR.

peter-the-great.name: Peter the Great
peter-the-great.summary: Tsar of Russia from 1682 and its first emperor from 1721 until his death in 1725, who westernized Russia, built its navy, and founded St Petersburg.

irtysh.name: Irtysh
irtysh.summary: A river flowing through Russia, China and Kazakhstan, the chief tributary of the Ob and the longest tributary in the world.

dzungar-khanate.name: Dzungar Khanate
dzungar-khanate.summary: The last nomadic empire, founded by Oirat Mongols, stretching at its height from southern Siberia to Tibet; it conquered Tibet in 1717 before being destroyed by the Qing dynasty between 1755 and 1758.

omsk.name: Omsk
omsk.summary: Administrative center of Omsk Oblast in southwestern Siberia, Russia, with a population over one million; briefly served as capital of the anti-Bolshevik Russian State during the Russian Civil War (1918–1920).

yarkant-county.name: Yarkand
yarkant-county.summary: A Silk Road oasis city in the Tarim Basin (now in Xinjiang), once seat of an ancient Buddhist kingdom and later capital of the Yarkand Khanate, fed by the Yarkand River.

afaq-khoja.name: Afaq Khoja
afaq-khoja.summary: A Naqshbandi Sufi leader holding the title Khwaja who also ruled as a political leader in Kashgaria, in present-day southern Xinjiang, also known by his birth name Hidayat Allah.

revolt-of-the-altishahr-khojas.name: Burhan al-Din
revolt-of-the-altishahr-khojas.summary: One of two Khoja brothers, nicknamed 'Elder Khoja,' who took part in a 1757 uprising against the Qing dynasty in Altishahr alongside his brother after being freed from Dzungar captivity.

galdan-boshugtu-khan.name: Galdan Boshugtu Khan
galdan-boshugtu-khan.summary: A Choros-Oirat khan of the Dzungar Khanate (1644–1697), son of its founder Erdeni Batur and a descendant of the 15th-century Oirat ruler Esen Taishi.

alexander-bekovich-cherkassky.name: Alexander Bekovich-Cherkassky
alexander-bekovich-cherkassky.summary: A Russian officer of Circassian origin, born Devlet-Girei-mırza, who died in 1717 after leading Russia's first military expedition into Central Asia.

oskemen.name: Ust-Kamenogorsk
oskemen.summary: The largest city in eastern Kazakhstan, also known as Öskemen, and administrative center of the East Kazakhstan Region.

kazan.name: Kazan
kazan.summary: Capital of Tatarstan, Russia, on the Volga River; formerly capital of the Khanate of Kazan until conquered by Ivan the Terrible in the 16th century.

yemelyan-pugachev.name: Yemelyan Pugachev
yemelyan-pugachev.summary: A Cossack ataman (c.1742-1775) who led a major uprising against Catherine the Great, claiming to be her dead husband Peter III, before being captured and executed in Moscow.

j-z.name: Jüz
j-z.summary: One of three tribal divisions (also called hordes) of the Kazakhs — Senior, Middle and Junior jüz — each covering a different region of Kazakhstan and neighboring lands.

clear-script.name: Clear Script
clear-script.summary: Alphabet created in 1648 by the Oirat monk Zaya Pandita, based on the Mongolian script, designed to capture every sound of the Oirat language precisely.

oirats.name: Oirats
oirats.summary: The westernmost group of Mongols, originally from the Altai region of Siberia, Xinjiang and western Mongolia; today's Kalmyks of southeastern Europe descend from them.

mongolian-script.name: Mongolian script
mongolian-script.summary: The traditional vertical Mongolian alphabet, derived from the Old Uyghur script, the main way of writing Mongolian until Cyrillic replaced it in 1946.

epic-of-manas.name: Epic of Manas
epic-of-manas.summary: A traditional epic poem of the Kyrgyz people, developed over centuries through oral tradition and considered the longest epic poem ever recorded, with over two million words in its most famous version.

galik-alphabet.name: Galik alphabet
galik-alphabet.summary: A 1587 extension to the traditional Mongolian script adding characters for transcribing Tibetan, Sanskrit, and later Chinese terms in religious translations; some are still used for foreign names.

3rd-dalai-lama.name: Sonam Gyatso
3rd-dalai-lama.summary: Sonam Gyatso (1543-1588), the first to formally hold the title Dalai Lama, granted by Altan Khan in 1578; he spread Tibetan Buddhism into Mongolia and founded several monasteries.

classical-mongolian.name: Classical Mongolian
classical-mongolian.summary: A literary Mongolian language introduced after 1600 to translate the Tibetan Buddhist canon, used for Mongolian literature until the 1930s.

kangyur.name: Kangyur
kangyur.summary: The collection of Buddha's recorded teachings within the Tibetan Buddhist canon, distinct from the Tengyur commentaries, studied across Tibetan and Mongolian Buddhism.

tengyur.name: Tengyur
tengyur.summary: A collection of commentaries by Buddhist masters on the Buddha's teachings, forming part of the Tibetan Buddhist Canon alongside the Kangyur.

altan-tobchi.name: Altan Tobchi
altan-tobchi.summary: 17th-century Mongolian chronicle that preserves most of the Secret History of the Mongols, ranked second only to it in importance to Mongolian literature.

secret-history-of-the-mongols.name: Secret History of the Mongols
secret-history-of-the-mongols.summary: The oldest surviving literary work in Mongolic languages, written for the Mongol royal family after Genghis Khan's death in 1227 to recount his life, conquests, and part of his successor's reign.

khoshut.name: Khoshut
khoshut.summary: One of the four major tribes of the Oirat Mongols, who established the Khoshut Khanate in the Qinghai region from 1642 to 1717.

khalkha-mongols.name: Khalkha Mongols
khalkha-mongols.summary: The largest subgroup of the Mongols in present-day Mongolia since the 15th century, historically ruled directly by Borjigin khans and making up most of Mongolia's population today.

arthur-thomas-hatto.name: Arthur Thomas Hatto
arthur-thomas-hatto.summary: English scholar of German studies at the University of London (1910–2010), known for translating medieval German poems such as Tristan and Parzival and for his theory of epic heroic poetry.

soyombo-script.name: Soyombo script
soyombo-script.summary: An alphabet invented in 1686 by Mongolian Buddhist monk Zanabazar to write Mongolian, Tibetan and Sanskrit; its symbol later became a national emblem of Mongolia.

jami-al-tawarikh.name: Jami' al-Tawarikh
jami-al-tawarikh.summary: Early 14th-century work often called 'the first world history,' written by Rashid al-Din for the Mongol Ilkhanate and covering cultures from China to Europe.

diwan-poetry.name: Diwan (poetry)
diwan-poetry.summary: Tradition of poetry collections by a single author across Islamic cultures of West and Central Asia, North Africa and South Asia, dominated by lyric forms such as ghazals.

ali-shir-nava-i.name: Ali-Shir Nava'i
ali-shir-nava-i.summary: Timurid poet, writer and statesman (1441–1501) regarded as the founder of early Turkic literature, who argued his native Chagatai Turkic surpassed Persian for poetry.

dornod-province.name: Dornod Province
dornod-province.summary: The easternmost of Mongolia's 21 provinces, with its capital at Choibalsan.

hanlin-academy.name: Hanlin Academy
hanlin-academy.summary: An elite institution founded in 8th-century Tang China where scholars did literary work for the court and helped shape the imperial examination system.

ob.name: Ob
ob.summary: A major river in western Siberia, Russia, forming with its tributary the Irtysh the world's seventh-longest river system, flowing into the Arctic Ocean.

yenisei.name: Yenisei
yenisei.summary: The fifth-longest river system in the world and the largest draining into the Arctic Ocean, flowing north through central Siberia; its basin includes Lake Baikal, the world's deepest lake.

lena-river.name: Lena River
lena-river.summary: A 4,294-km river in Russian Siberia flowing north into the Arctic Ocean, the longest river entirely within Russia and eleventh-longest in the world.

erdene-zuu-monastery.name: Erdene Zuu Monastery
erdene-zuu-monastery.summary: Likely Mongolia's earliest surviving Buddhist monastery, built in 1585 in Kharkhorin and affiliated with the Gelug sect of Tibetan Buddhism; now part of a World Heritage Site.

kharkhorin.name: Kharkhorin
kharkhorin.summary: A town in Mongolia near the ruins of Karakorum, the Mongol Empire's 13th-century capital under Ogedei Khan, and home to the Erdene Zuu Monastery.

v-rkhangai-province.name: Övörkhangai Province
v-rkhangai-province.summary: A province of Mongolia, home to important monasteries including Erdene Zuu, located near the site of Karakorum, the ancient Mongol Empire capital.

tobolsk.name: Tobolsk
tobolsk.summary: A town founded in 1587 at the confluence of the Tobol and Irtysh rivers, the second-oldest Russian settlement east of the Urals and historic capital of Siberia.

khanate-of-sibir.name: Khanate of Sibir
khanate-of-sibir.summary: A Siberian Tatar state in western Siberia formed after the Golden Horde's breakup, ruled by rival dynasties descended from Genghis Khan; its defeat by Yermak in 1582 began Russia's conquest of Siberia.

ket-river.name: Ket River
ket-river.summary: A 1,621-kilometre river in Siberia flowing west into the Ob, once a key trade route with a portage linking it to the Yenisei basin.

yeniseysk.name: Yeniseysk
yeniseysk.summary: A town in Krasnoyarsk Krai, Russia, located on the Yenisei River.

tobol.name: Tobol River
tobol.summary: A 1,591 km river in Western Siberia (Kazakhstan and Russia) and the main left tributary of the Irtysh.

kama-river.name: Kama River
kama-river.summary: A 1,805-kilometre river in Russia, the longest and largest left tributary of the Volga, flowing from Udmurtia through Perm Krai and Tatarstan to join the Volga near Kazan.

mangazeya.name: Mangazeya
mangazeya.summary: A Russian trading town founded in 1601 in northwestern Siberia, abandoned by 1672 and now an archaeological site.

taz-river.name: Taz River
taz-river.summary: A 1,401-kilometer river in western Siberia; the now-ruined trading city of Mangazeya once stood on its banks.

yakutsk.name: Yakutsk
yakutsk.summary: The capital of Sakha, Russia, located south of the Arctic Circle on the Lena River, known as the coldest major city in the world.

muhammad-shaybani.name: Shaybani Khan
muhammad-shaybani.summary: Uzbek leader (c. 1451–1510) who united Uzbek tribes and laid the foundations for the Khanate of Bukhara in Transoxiana.

herat.name: Herat
herat.summary: Ancient city in western Afghanistan on the Silk Road that became a major center of the Timurid Renaissance after being conquered by Timur.

timurid-dynasty.name: Timurid dynasty
timurid-dynasty.summary: The Turco-Mongol ruling family of the Timurid Empire, descended from Timur, whose members also founded the Mughal Empire and called themselves Gurkani, meaning 'son-in-law'.

khorasan.name: Khorasan
khorasan.summary: A historical region of the Iranian Plateau spanning parts of modern Afghanistan, Iran and Central Asia, with boundaries that varied over time and roots reaching back to Bronze Age complex societies there.

kazakh-khanate.name: Kazakh Khanate
kazakh-khanate.summary: A nomadic Central Asian state lasting from about 1465 to the early 19th century, formed after the breakup of the Golden Horde.

tauke-khan.name: Tauke Khan
tauke-khan.summary: Kazakh khan who ruled the Kazakh Khanate from 1680 to 1715, keeping its three juzes unified and earning the title 'Shah-i-Turan' while making contact with Peter I of Russia.

chinggisids.name: Chinggisids
chinggisids.summary: The descendants of Genghis Khan and his wife Börte, who by tradition were considered the only legitimate rulers of the Mongol Empire and its successor states, a rule that lasted until 1847.

later-jin-1616-1636.name: Later Jin
later-jin-1616-1636.summary: A Jurchen-led dynasty established in Manchuria in 1616 by Nurhaci, renamed Great Qing in 1636 to begin the Qing dynasty.

northern-yuan.name: Northern Yuan
northern-yuan.summary: Mongol Borjigin dynastic state on the Mongolian Plateau, a rump state formed after the Yuan dynasty's collapse in 1368 and conquered by the Later Jin dynasty in 1635.

mongol-eight-banners.name: Mongol Eight Banners
mongol-eight-banners.summary: Hereditary military and administrative units of Mongol bannermen in the Qing dynasty, formally established in 1635 alongside the Manchu and Han Chinese Eight Banners.

hong-taiji.name: Hong Taiji
hong-taiji.summary: Second khan of the Later Jin dynasty and founding emperor of the Qing dynasty (1592 to 1643), who conquered Inner Mongolia and Manchuria and made Korea a Qing tributary.

kharchin-mongols.name: Kharchin Mongols
kharchin-mongols.summary: A Mongol subgroup living mainly in northeastern China, descended from Ming-era border guards who merged around 1600 and were later organized into banners under the Manchus in 1626.

jurchen-people.name: Jurchen
jurchen-people.summary: Tungusic-speaking peoples of northeastern China who founded the Jin and Qing dynasties; they were renamed Manchus in 1635 by Hong Taiji.

babur.name: Babur
babur.summary: Founder of the Mughal Empire in South Asia (1483–1530), a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan who conquered Kabul in 1504 and defeated the Sultan of Delhi in 1526.

ulugh-beg-ii.name: Ulugh Beg II
ulugh-beg-ii.summary: The Timurid ruler of Kabul and Ghazni from 1461 until his death in 1502.

delhi-sultanate.name: Delhi Sultanate
delhi-sultanate.summary: A late medieval empire based in Delhi that ruled large parts of the Indian subcontinent for over three centuries from 1206, through five dynasties ending with the Lodi in 1526.

anna-of-russia.name: Empress Anna
anna-of-russia.summary: Empress of Russia from 1730 to 1740, niece of Peter the Great, whose reign continued his Westernizing projects but is often remembered in Russia as a 'dark era'.

lifan-yuan.name: Lifan Yuan
lifan-yuan.summary: A Qing dynasty government agency that administered China's Inner Asian territories such as Mongolia and Tibet, and handled relations with Russia until the 1860s.

yuan-dynasty.name: Yuan dynasty
yuan-dynasty.summary: A Mongol-led dynasty ruling China from 1271 to 1368, founded by Kublai Khan, and the first non-Han dynasty to rule all of China.

panchen-lama.name: Panchen Lama
panchen-lama.summary: A leading figure of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, second in spiritual authority only to the Dalai Lama, with the title dating to 1645.

abtai-sain-khan.name: Abtai Sain Khan
abtai-sain-khan.summary: Khalkha Mongolian prince (1554–1588) named the first khan of the Tüsheet Khanate in 1587, who spread Tibetan Buddhism among the Khalkha Mongols and founded Erdene Zuu monastery in 1585.

karakorum.name: Karakorum
karakorum.summary: Capital of the Mongol Empire from 1235 to 1260 and later of the Northern Yuan dynasty, founded in 1220 in what is now Mongolia.

naqshbandi-order.name: Naqshbandi Order
naqshbandi-order.summary: A major Sufi order within Sunni Islam founded in the 14th century by Baha' al-Din Naqshband, known for strict adherence to Islamic law and silent devotional practices.

yarkent-khanate.name: Yarkand Khanate
yarkent-khanate.summary: A Sunni Muslim khanate ruled by Turkified Mongol descendants of Genghis Khan, founded in 1514 after conquering Kashgar, Yarkent and Hotan, and conquered by the Dzungar Khanate in 1705.

khong-tayiji.name: Khong Tayiji
khong-tayiji.summary: A Mongol title meaning crown prince, originally reserved for descendants of Genghis Khan, later used as a sub-khan rank and, by the mid-18th century, ranked above khan among the Oirats.

erdeni-batur.name: Erdeni Batur
erdeni-batur.summary: A Choros-Oirat prince (died 1653) generally regarded as founder of the Dzungar Khanate, centred in the Dzungaria region of what is now north-westernmost China.

lobsang-ch-kyi-gyaltsen-4th-panchen-lama.name: 4th Panchen Lama
lobsang-ch-kyi-gyaltsen-4th-panchen-lama.summary: The fourth Panchen Lama of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism (1570-1662), teacher and close ally of the 5th Dalai Lama, who gave him Tashilhunpo Monastery.

kalmyks.name: Kalmyks
kalmyks.summary: A Mongolic people in Europe descended from Oirats who migrated from Dzungaria in early modern times and founded the Kalmyk Khanate in the 17th century; Europe's only traditionally Buddhist ethnic group.

genghis-khan.name: Genghis Khan
genghis-khan.summary: Founder of the Mongol Empire (c. 1162-1227), who united the Mongol tribes and conquered large parts of China and Central Asia.

4th-dalai-lama.name: Yonten Gyatso
4th-dalai-lama.summary: The 4th Dalai Lama (1589-1617), a Mongol and great-grandson of Altan Khan, making him one of only two non-Tibetans ever recognized as Dalai Lama.
